The Pali Tradition on the Noble Person Who is a “Body-witness” (kāya-sakkhin), and the Nature of “Witnessing”and the “Body” in the Samādhi States in Which They Excel
papers.abstract: This article explores the “body-witness” (kāya-sakkhin), one of the types of person who are “noble ones” (ariyas): people with different levels of enlightenment on the noble path. It begins by examining the types of noble ones and how they differ, to focus on what is particular to the body-witness. This is their emphasis on samādhi, meditative concentration, rather than on faith or wisdom. They are seen to excel in the four meditative absorptions known as jhānas, the four formless states, and the cessation of perception and feeling. They experience these in a deeper way than the freed-by-wisdom type of arahat (who can also experience these states to a degree), but in a similar way to the freed-both-ways arahat. Analysis of relevant canonical passages show that jhānas and formless states can be experienced in a range of depths and with different degrees of accompanying wisdom. Then, after examining the nature of “witnessing” in the suttas, the range of meanings of kāya is analysed: the physical body, the tactile sense, a route of action, the body of mental states other than consciousness, the sentient body that encompasses these and the physical body, and also all aspects of a person, all five khandhas. A key aspect of the jhānas is that joy and happiness, then just happiness, then an equanimous mindful mind, completely pervade the experienced, sensed body. Hence jhāna very much involves the body, in a positive way. The formless states which build on the jhānas, though, are purely mental states, beyond any sense-impressions or ideas related to material form. Here the mental body comes to the fore, yet in cessation mental states may completely cease, leaving just a living physical body. So “body-witnessing” works in a range of ways but, for a body-witness then freed-both-ways person, in a very deep way in which there is a direct mindful “touching” of the states of samādhi, so as to be in close “contact” with them. This also provides a basis for a further range of “witnessing” in the “higher knowledges” in which the body and sensing are seen to go far beyond their usual range.

papers.title: Why Should Sīla Lead to Samādhi? Hindrances, Pleasure, and the Transformation of Mind in Early Buddhism
papers.abstract: Why should sīla lead to samādhi? If samādhi is interpreted as an independently trainable capacity for sustained concentration, its systematic dependence on ethical and motivational cultivation is difficult to explain. I argue that, in relevant Nikāya contexts, being samāhita need not be constituted by a particular relation between mind and object, including the exclusive occupation of consciousness by a single determinate content. Cognitive workability and readiness for purposive use may instead identify a more general functional feature of being samāhita, without excluding states of intense deliberate engagement with a particular object. Against this background, I examine the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) as a possible bridge between conduct, samādhi, and understanding. Several hindrances do more than distract attention: they express motivational pressures that recruit cognition toward acquisition, resistance, reconsideration, or resolution. Disciplined conduct, sense restraint, moderation, and related practices can progressively weaken the motivational dispositions from which these pressures arise. Their weakening can therefore contribute directly to the mind’s becoming gathered and workable by reducing processes that repeatedly pre-empt cognition. The same transformation also has an affective dimension. In the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, recognition of the abandonment of the hindrances gives rise to pāmojja, pīti, tranquillity, and sukha. Drawing also on the Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta, I suggest that this experience can do more than reinforce an intellectual understanding of the drawbacks of sensuality that remains soteriologically insufficient. When the desired object remains unobtained while wanting itself subsides and wellbeing nevertheless improves, the practitioner encounters potentially transformative experiential evidence concerning the causal structure of dukkha: what appeared to be a felt deficiency—one important form of dukkha—caused by the absence of the desired object may instead have been produced or intensified by the desire itself. The resulting model presents sīla, the absence of the hindrances, affective transformation, samādhi, and understanding as dynamically connected aspects of a single developmental process and helps explain why ethical discipline can progressively reduce both motivational disturbance and the need for continuous effortful regulation.

papers.title: Health effects of Sahaj Samadhi meditation: A scoping review of evidence across cognitive, neurophysiological and clinical domains.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Mental health disorders contribute to disability worldwide. Chronic stress can lead to cardiovascular diseases, metabolic syndrome, and immune dysfunction, posing a major public health challenge. Meditation-based approaches improve stress resilience and overall wellbeing. Sahaj Samadhi Meditation (SSM) is a mantra-based meditative practice, with a limited but emerging evidence base. This scoping review aimed to summarise the existing evidence.


METHODS
Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) and the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology (JBI), we searched PubMed, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and Scopus (from inception to July 2026), along with clinical trial registries. Studies assessing SSM as the primary intervention were included. Screening and data extraction were conducted independently by two reviewers. The protocol was registered in the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/2rckd).


RESULTS
Eleven studies were included: five experimental studies, one community survey, two clinical intervention studies, and three registered protocols. Experimental studies showed consistent differences in attentional processing, perceptual stability, and neurophysiological markers, including higher frontal theta coherence and increased mismatch negativity responses among SSM practitioners. Patients with glaucoma and chronic pain reported modest improvements in sleep quality and depressive symptoms. Protocols evaluate late-life depression, opioid-related outcomes and chronic pain in SSM practitioners. All studies were small with substantial heterogeneity.


CONCLUSIONS
SSM may influence psychological, neurophysiological, and cognitive parameters. However, these findings are based on small samples with narrow evidence base. Large trials with standardised protocols are required to recommend SSM for clinical use or integrate into community-based health programmes.

The Supreme Yoga and the Science of Suggestion: Bridging the Yoga Vasistha and Modern Hypnotherapy Through Consciousness, Narrative, and Neuroscience
papers.abstract: The Yoga Vasistha (Moksopaya), among the most psychologically sophisticated works of Indian philosophy, teaches that experienced worlds are mind-made, that latent impressions (vasana) sustain suffering, that disciplined imagination (bhavana) and self-effort can dissolve them, and that liberation is available in life (jivanmukti). Modern hypnotherapy - whose founding doctrine of suggestion entered Europe through the Goa-born Abbe Faria, whose largest early clinical corpus was produced in Bengal, and whose first theorist, James Braid, analysed reports of yogic samadhi - has independently validated the operative core of these claims across a meta-analytic evidence base. This article presents the first systematic integration of the two traditions and introduces Yoga Vasistha Hypnotherapy (YVH), an integrative clinical model. Using a method of complementarity without collapse, we map thirteen construct concordances, align the seven jnana-bhumikas with graded trance depths as a heuristic clinical map, and identify the text's jivanmukta with Fundamental Peace - an integrated regulatory capacity comprising flexible attentional control, emotional coherence, reduced self-referential rigidity and compassionate self-awareness, measurable by the FP20 scale. We state the model's disanalogies and cultural-integrity commitments, derive an eight-phase protocol, and propose five testable hypotheses, returning the science of suggestion to its deepest source while giving contemplative clinical practice a validated endpoint.

papers.title: Buddhist Principles of Self-Management: Integrating Morality, Mindfulness, and Wisdom into Modern Leadership and Organizational Practice
papers.abstract: This paper offers a redefined, self-management through the lens of ethics, drawing on the early Buddhist canonical texts. By employing a qualitative thematic methodology from focused studies of the, Dīgha Nikāya; Majjhima Nikāya; and, Aṅguttara Nikāya, this study seeks to define self-management as a cohesive, systemic construct that consists of ethical discipline (sīla), mental discipline (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā), and is undergirded by mindfulness (sati) and non-attachment (virāga). The findings reveal that self-management as ethical self-governance is early Buddhism’s perspective as opposed to the understanding of self-management as a neutral and psychological phenomenon. Sila establishes, the self-restraint, moral accountability and trust in the social system; samādhi helps to stabilize attention along with the regulation of emotional reactivity; and, paññā assists in turbulent times with respect to the, reflection under conditions of, complexity and ambiguity. Sati serves as ethical vigilance; allowing persons to unwholesome volitional impulses, and, unwholesome, voluntary impulses to act, while, virāga counteracts ego involvement, fixation on outcomes, and, assists, with ethical consistency under pressure. These sets are viewed as operating situationally as system. Re-establishing both the ethical and epistemic coherence of Buddhist self-management, this study provides a conceptually sound alternative to the more instrumental and reductionist interpretations of mindfulness and emotional regulation. In leadership and organizational studies, it advances an integrated model of ethical self-regulation that considers the interplay of the three components of Buddhism, i.e., morality, emotional regulation, and wisdom, without collapsing Buddhist doctrine to instrumentalist ends.

papers.title: Unlooping the self: Ego dissolution and the collapse of recursive identity.
papers.abstract: Ego dissolution—the experience of losing one’s sense of self—is reported across a range of altered states, including psychedelic intoxication, meditative absorption, traumatic dissociation, and psychotic episodes. This paper proposes a unifying framework for these phenomena by introducing the concept of unlooping: the breakdown of recursive structures that construct and maintain identity. Drawing on models of recursive self-modeling, predictive processing, and enactive cognition, ego dissolution is interpreted as a graded suspension of feedback loops responsible for agency, continuity, and self-boundary. Through phenomenological analysis and cross-contextual case studies, the paper demonstrates that selfhood is not an ontological constant but a contingent, dynamically enacted achievement. Unlooping the self reveals both the fragility and plasticity of identity and offers new insights into the intersection of subjective experience and cognitive architecture. The implications span theoretical, methodological, and therapeutic domains, suggesting a revised account of selfhood that incorporates its capacity for suspension and reorganization

papers.title: Neural architecture of the jhānas: a gamma-infraslow duet with quantum overtones
papers.abstract:
Building on previous electrophysiological investigations that posited meditative absorption (jhāna) as a radical disruption of sensory default consciousness (DCs), this study explores the underlying non-linear neural architectures and state transitions. Re-analysis of long-duration (

A broadband (0.005–150 Hz) 3D eLoreta source analysis of a major 4,000 µV relaxation-oscillation (R-O) transition into the second jhāna, confirms the active silencing of fronto-temporal linguistic networks, leading to the profound mental stillness characteristic of higher absorption states. This macro state transition is driven by a near-absolute variance concentration of infraslow rhythms localized to the midline vertex (

This coordinated gamma–infraslow duet constructs an impenetrable, low-entropy Markov blanket, actively insulating the internal cognitive field from sensory perturbation while maintaining waking alertness. Concurrently, the 600-fold deceleration of cortical rhythms at the vertex facilitates heightened synchrony with visceral neurovascular systems. At critical R-O inflection thresholds, brief (1–2 s) global high-gamma microbursts function as inhibitory sweeps across left-lateralized hubs (BA 47, BA 21/22/38), dismantling emerging inner speech to protect absorptive stability. The study further demonstrates that the jhāna hierarchy follows a scale-free trajectory distinct from the θ, α, β frequency bands of default sensory consciousness (DCs), bypassing the 1 Hz deep-sleep transition, replacing nested sensory Markov blankets with a singular global boundary at the fourth-jhāna limit—a system with intriguing similarities to noise-shielded quantum “superposition.” We conclude that jhāna consciousness (JCs) constitutes an autonomous and previously unrecognized, highly structured second-tier of human consciousness, rather than an altered state of (sensory) consciousness (ASC).

papers.title: Advanced meditation stabilizes cortical dynamics through inhibitory gain control linked to absorptive depth
papers.abstract: Advanced meditation can shift conscious experience from ordinary body- and world-centered awareness toward absorption, detachment and dissociation-like states, yet the neural mechanisms that stabilize these immersive states remain unclear. We studied 18 long-term meditators during eyes-open rest and Rajyoga meditation, a practice in which practitioners reduce bodily identification while enhancing inner self-awareness. We combined multidimensional neural approach including frontal EEG spectral power, temporal non-stationarity and corticothalamic neural-field modeling, because these measures probe underlying complementary levels of the brain state transition: the strength of neural activity, its temporal stability, and the circuit level inhibition-excitation gain mechanisms. This framework is especially relevant to meditation because oscillatory, temporal organization may distinguish stable meditative states, and corticothalamic dynamics are closely linked to arousal and conscious state regulation. We correlated meditation induced neural changes with subjective ratings of absorption and dissociation. Compared with rest, meditation was associated with higher beta1, beta2 and gamma power, with no change in the slower bands (delta, theta and alpha), and with lower beta-band temporal non-stationarity, indicating a more stable expression of fast cortical dynamics. Fitting the corticothalamic model to the EEG spectra showed stronger cortical inhibitory gain and lower effective intracortical gain, placing meditation in an inhibition-dominant regime, with lower gain in the loop between excitatory and inhibitory neurons within the cortex. During meditation, these model estimates were related to subjective absorption and showed trend level links with dissociation. Together, these findings suggest that Rajyoga meditation stabilizes cortical dynamics through inhibitory gain control, linking absorption (deep and steady attention on the meditation) to dissociation-like self-detachment.

papers.title: Low‐Frequency Microwave Absorption Composites
papers.abstract: Electromagnetic wave devices and components operating in the low‐frequency band of 1–8 GHz (L, S, and C bands) are widely applied in wireless data communication systems, satellite radar, and other fields. However, traditional low‐frequency microwave absorption materials (MAMs) suffer from issues such as large thickness, heavy weight, difficult impedance matching, insufficient low‐frequency microwave loss, and poor environmental stability, severely limiting use and development. In recent years, researchers construct composite systems combining various types of loss, coupled with component adjustments and structural design strategies, significantly improving the impedance matching and multiple loss synergy effects for low‐frequency MAMs. Based on the above, this review briefly introduces the basic principle of microwave absorption and the influence factors of low‐frequency microwave absorption performance, and systematically reviews the recent research progress of carbon‐based composites, magnetics‐based composites, polymer‐based composites, ceramic‐based composites, and multiphase hybrid composites. Additionally, the intrinsic relationship and mechanisms are discussed in detail between the micro‐structure and macro‐performance of different composites. Furthermore, the key scientific and technical bottleneck problems that need to be addressed in the design and preparation of low‐frequency MAMs are identified. It is expected to provide theoretical guidance for the controlled preparation and performance regulation of low‐frequency microwave absorption composites.

papers.title: The effects of active recovery and meditation on perceived fatigue, cognitive function, and physical performance following mental fatigue: A randomised crossover study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Mental fatigue is a psychophysiological state caused by periods of prolonged cognitively demanding activity, characterised by impaired motivation, cognitive, and physical performance. Whether mental fatigue also affects functional movement ability, and the extent to which recovery strategies such as active recovery, meditation, or passive recovery mitigate these effects, remains unclear. METHODS: This study examined the impact of active recovery, meditation, and passive recovery on perceptions of fatigue, cognitive and physical performance, and movement ability. Using a repeated-measures randomised crossover design, 12 healthy young adults completed perceptual, cognitive, functional, and performance tests before and after a 30-minute Stroop task. Participants then completed 15 minutes of active recovery, meditation, or passive recovery in a randomised order across three sessions before repeating the tests. Data were analysed using linear mixed-effects models and cumulative link mixed models. RESULTS: The Stroop task induced large increases in perceived physical and mental fatigue (ηp2 = 0.267-0.497), slowed Go/No-Go response time (ηp2 = 0.301), and reduced hurdle step and in-line lunge movement quality, alongside a moderate reduction in knee extensor force (ηp2 = 0.094). N-back accuracy changed little, although a ceiling effect limited the capacity to detect change. Time × intervention interaction effects were small to moderate (ηp2 = 0.016 to 0.080) and largely compatible with the null. Outcomes generally returned towards baseline during the 15-minute recovery period in all conditions, with minimal evidence that active recovery or meditation produced greater recovery than passive rest; responses varied considerably between individuals. CONCLUSION: A 30-minute Stroop task acutely increased fatigue, as evidenced by changes in perceptual, cognitive, functional, and performance outcomes. Outcomes generally moved back towards baseline over the 15-minute recovery period regardless of modality, with minimal evidence that active recovery or meditation offered greater benefit than passive rest. These exploratory findings require confirmation in larger samples.

papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study evaluated the feasibility and acceptability of the iQuit Mindfully app for smoking cessation among adults with low socioeconomic status (SES). METHOD: In this 12-week feasibility study, 62 adults with low SES (58% female, 94% annual household income <200% federal poverty level, 48% White, 39% Black,  RESULTS: Whereas participants in both conditions provided positive feedback, iQuit Mindfully participants uniquely highlighted the benefits of mindfulness for managing stress and cravings. Benchmarks for retention (80%; actual 93%) and acceptability (7 on a 1-10 scale) were exceeded. iQuit Mindfully participants were more likely to recommend the app ( CONCLUSIONS: Results support the acceptability of the iQuit Mindfully app for adults with low SES. Participant feedback will be used to improve the app with the long-term goal to provide accessible smoking cessation support for low-SES adults. papers.title: Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction and Psychological Distress Among Saudi University Nursing Students.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Nursing students often experience high levels of psychological distress that can negatively affect their mental health, academic performance, and future clinical practice. METHOD: An experimental study was conducted with 106 nursing students who showed elevated psychological distress. Participants were randomly allocated into an intervention group receiving mindfulness-based stress reduction and a control group using a 1:1 ratio. RESULTS: Repeated measures analyses of covariance revealed significant reductions in mean depression, anxiety, and stress scores in the intervention group compared with the control group, with  CONCLUSION: The findings suggest that regular mindfulness practice can improve student wellness and academic functioning. Integrating mindfulness-based stress reduction into nursing education can provide an evidence-based, culturally adaptable method to lower psychological distress and enhance mental health support in Saudi universities.

papers.title: Sustainable Caregiving: Feasibility and Preliminary Results of a Skill-Building Course for Care Partners of Patients with Cancer.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Caregiving for patients with serious illness can increase morbidity and mortality on care partners and worsen patient outcomes. There is a vital need to support care partners. METHODS: A chaplain-led, eight-week skill-building course was conducted for 31 care partners of patients with cancer at a comprehensive cancer center. Care partner resiliency, self-efficacy, and burnout were measured before and after the course ( RESULTS: Participants reported increased resilience ( CONCLUSION: This chaplain-led, online skill-building course demonstrated the potential for improved resilience, decreased burnout, and increased self-efficacy in care partners. Exploration of the course's potential impacts on long-term care partner outcomes in a larger study is needed.

papers.title: Singing into Presence: Exploring a Spiritually Informed Music Therapy Approach for Self-Reflection, Present-Moment Awareness and Mental Wellbeing with an Australian University Population.
papers.abstract: Attention is necessary for effective learning and disruptions in attention may occur with stress. This study explored the feasibility of Active Voice Yoga (AVY), a spiritually informed culturally adapted music and meditation approach, applied in clinical music therapy to support attention, self-awareness and wellbeing in emerging adults. Central to the investigation of the music therapy intervention, the mechanism of a musically guided self-reflective process examined impacts of mental silence meditation on attention and mental wellbeing. The qualitative study involved the applied clinical intervention of AVY with an Australian university population experiencing typical stressors (N = 11; 6 female, 4 male, 1 non-binary). The exploratory online programme employed music therapist guided singing of bija mantras and affirmations combined with music listening and meditation. Using an interpretative qualitative approach, surveys and interviews captured rich subjective data on participants' physical, mental, emotional, and unique experiences. Thematic analysis revealed positive outcomes regarding the applicability of the vocal method, perceived as an accessible, easy-to-use and efficient mechanism for stabilising attention and emotions. The spiritually derived vocal tools, adapted for secular therapeutic use, facilitated strong experiences of present-moment awareness and transcendent meditative states associated with stress reduction and emotional regulation. The study provides detailed insight into real-time experiences of meditation and how active musical mechanisms support present-moment awareness, maintenance of thought-free meditative states and enhanced attentional attributes. Findings contribute to the research base establishing user-friendly methods employing the voice for wellbeing in clinical therapeutic practice and applying a mental silence meditation approach to supporting attentional capacities, spiritual wellbeing and mental health.

papers.title: Effects of different cognition-oriented therapies for cognitive impairment: A network meta-analysis of randomized trials.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The comparative effectiveness of various cognitive interventions for older adults with cognitive impairment remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to evaluate and rank cognition-oriented therapies for individuals with mild-to-moderate cognitive impairment. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and network meta‑analysis of RCTs from nine databases up to August 2025, using random‑effects models. We assessed transitivity, heterogeneity, and consistency (global and local), as well as publication bias; sensitivity and subgroup analyses were also performed. The certainty of evidence was rated using GRADE. RESULTS: 49 RCTs (2968 participants) included. On MMSE, CT (SMD=0.81), CCT (0.49), CST (0.26), and RT (0.32) improved vs control; CRT and VR not significant; MBCT inferior (-0.45). On MoCA, CT (0.58) and CCT (0.54) superior. No global inconsistency, but local inconsistency for VR vs CRT (P = 0.039). SUCRA: CT first (90.4%) and CCT second (87.5%) for MMSE; RT first (94.0%) for MoCA but based on only two studies with high heterogeneity. Sensitivity analysis excluding high‑risk studies substantially reordered rankings (MBCT rose to second). CONCLUSION: CT and CCT showed the most consistent cognitive benefits across outcomes. However, the evidence was of low-to-moderate certainty, and rankings were fragile and sensitive to study quality. The apparent advantage of RT in the MoCA analysis was based on very limited data and is unreliable. Individualized care is advisable, but current evidence is insufficient to inform practice guidelines. Future high-quality trials are essential.

papers.title: Non-pharmacological interventions for anxiety and pain in thyroid fine-needle aspiration biopsy: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Thyroid fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) is the diagnostic standard for evaluating thyroid nodules but commonly provokes procedural anxiety and pain, which may contribute to non-diagnostic cytology, repeat procedures, and increased healthcare utilization. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the effectiveness of non-pharmacological interventions for reducing anxiety and pain during thyroid FNAB. METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were systematically searched from inception to May 2026 for randomized controlled trials comparing non-pharmacological interventions with usual care or no intervention in patients undergoing thyroid FNAB. Primary outcomes were post-procedural anxiety and anxiety change scores; pain was evaluated as a secondary outcome. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using standardized mean differences (SMDs). The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261411294). RESULTS: Seven randomized controlled trials involving 1,439 patients were included, with six contributing to the meta-analysis. Non-pharmacological interventions significantly reduced post-procedural anxiety (SMD = - 0.26; 95% CI, - 0.51 to - 0.01; p = 0.044; I² = 70.3%) and produced a greater pre- to post-procedure reduction in anxiety (change-score SMD = 0.57; 95% CI, 0.39 to 0.75; p < 0.0001; I² = 0%), where positive change-score values denote a larger reduction in anxiety in the intervention group. Video-based interventions showed a consistent moderate benefit, whereas music-based interventions did not significantly reduce post-procedural anxiety (test for subgroup differences, p = 0.005). Pain reduction was not statistically significant (SMD = - 0.49; 95% CI, - 1.23 to 0.25; p = 0.19; I² = 94.4%). One non-pooled trial found mindfulness reduced procedural adverse events and emotional stress. CONCLUSIONS: Non-pharmacological interventions, particularly video-based preparation, reduce anxiety during thyroid FNAB. Evidence for pain reduction remains inconclusive because of substantial heterogeneity. These findings support incorporating simple, low-cost interventions into routine thyroid FNAB while encouraging standardized protocols and further high-quality randomized trials.
